Shot size

Shot size numbers run upside down: the bigger the number, the smaller the pellet, so No. 9 is finer than No. 7½. The same number can mean slightly different sizes in Britain, continental Europe and the USA, so check the millimetres on the box. 'Nines' and 'seven-and-a-halfs' are common coach words.

  1. No. 9: about 2.0 mm.
  2. No. 8: about 2.2–2.3 mm.
  3. No. 7½: about 2.3–2.4 mm.
  4. No. 7: about 2.4–2.5 mm.

Why 'about'? Numbering differs between countries and makers. In the traditional British scale No. 7½ is 2.3 mm and No. 8 is 2.2 mm. Continental numbering, which some British makers such as Gamebore also use for clay loads, calls 2.4 mm shot No. 7½ and 2.3 mm shot No. 8. The American No. 7½ is 0.095 in, about 2.41 mm.

The rules of Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting require lead shot of round pellets of one size, 2.0 to 2.5 mm across (±0.1 mm). In practice that means No. 9, 8, 7½, and No. 7 if its diameter stays within the limit. No. 6 (about 2.6–2.8 mm) sits on the edge of the limit or beyond it, even with the tolerance, so it is not a competition load. Mixing shot of different sizes in one cartridge is forbidden.

Smaller shot gives more pellets for the same load: 28 g holds about 350–400 pellets of No. 7½, depending on the exact diameter, and about 580 of No. 9. So the pattern is denser, but each pellet is lighter and loses energy sooner.

That is why many shooters use No. 9 for close targets: its dense pattern covers the target easily. For medium and far targets they choose No. 8 or No. 7½, because heavier pellets break targets better at range. No. 7½ is also popular for tough rabbit targets and for a battue flying edge-on.

Tip: Many Sporting™ shooters pick one all-round cartridge, for example 28 g No. 7½ or No. 8, and keep things simple. Some load No. 9 in the first barrel for a close target and No. 7½ in the second.

Key points

  • Shot size: bigger number, smaller pellet; numbering differs by country, check millimetres.
  • No. 9 ≈ 2.0 mm, No. 8 ≈ 2.2–2.3 mm, No. 7½ ≈ 2.3–2.4 mm, No. 7 ≈ 2.4–2.5 mm
  • FITASC: round pellets of one size, 2.0 to 2.5 mm across (±0.1 mm); no mixing.
  • No. 9 for close targets, No. 8 and No. 7½ for medium and far ones.

Did you know?

Shot for clay cartridges is made of lead with some antimony added. Antimony makes the pellets harder, so they deform less in the barrel and give a more even pattern. Some shot is also nickel-plated.

Stand Talk

  • Coach Nines for the close stuff, seven-and-a-halfs for the long crossers.

    Meaning: Finer No. 9 shot for near targets, larger No. 7½ for far crossing targets.

For the interpreter
  • Say the shot number exactly as the coach gives it, and add the millimetres only if they are on the box.

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. Which is the finer shot?

    1. No. 7
    2. No. 7½
    3. No. 8
    4. No. 9
    Answer

    No. 9

    The bigger the shot number, the smaller the pellet.

  2. What shot diameter do the FITASC rules allow?

    1. 1.5–2.0 mm (±0.1 mm)
    2. 2.0–2.5 mm (±0.1 mm)
    3. 2.5–3.0 mm (±0.1 mm)
    4. Any size, if it is lead
    Answer

    2.0–2.5 mm (±0.1 mm)

    Shot must be round, lead and 2.0–2.5 mm across, with ±0.1 mm accepted.

    Chapter 7 · Cartridge rules

  3. Why is it better to look at the millimetres, not only at the shot number?

    1. The systems differ between countries
    2. Only dear cartridges show the number
    3. The number on the box means nothing
    4. The shot number shows the load, not size
    Answer

    The systems differ between countries

    The same number can differ by a tenth of a millimetre between systems.
